title: Rav Huna bar Avin
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Hyman describes this Amora as living in the Land of Israel, always mentioned as Rav Huna and not mentioned anywhere in the Jerusalem Talmud; he takes this as a sign that he was a Babylonian. He sent all his words from the Land of Israel to Babylonia, as in Rosh Hashanah 21a, where he sent to Rava: “When you see that the tekufah of Tevet extends,” etc.; Bava Batra 51a: “Rav Huna bar Avin sent: One who sells a field to his wife — she has acquired it … but Rabbi Abba, Rabbi Abbahu and all the great men of the generation said,” etc.; and there, 55b, he sent: “An Israelite who bought a field from an idolater … and so Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila and all our Rabbis are agreed on the matter,” etc. (all this Rav Huna bar Avin sent). In Nedarim 77b Rava said to Rav Nachman: “Let the Master see this scholar who came from the West and said that the Rabbis attended to the son of Rav Huna bar Avin and annulled his vows.” Hyman infers from this that Rabbi Avin without further designation was not his father, and that he lived in the Land of Israel in Rava’s time. From Bava Batra 51a, where he sent “but Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Abbahu” and did not mention Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi, Hyman takes this as a sign that this was after their death. He therefore interprets what they said in Kiddushin 8b — “The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant with coins … they came before Rabbi Ami” — as referring to the second Rabbi Ami, called Rabbi Ami the Babylonian, as explained in his entry. Seder HaDorot copied that they came before Rav Ashi, and an error issued from before him.
Hyman suggests that possibly he is the one mentioned in the Midrashim as Rabbi Huna HaKohen bar Avin; see his entry.

notes.text: Always RavHuna preserves Hyman’s title claim; the inference from absence in the Jerusalem Talmud, distinctions from Avin and Ami, and the death-based chronology remain Hyman’s. The final HunaHaKohen identification stays possible. No independent whole-corpus absence claim is made.

Rosh Hashanah 21a directly names Huna bar Avin sending the calendrical instruction to Rava. Hyman’s always-title assertion, inference from absence in the Jerusalem Talmud, later-Ami reconstruction and chronology from omitted names remain his. Possible identification with Huna HaKohen remains possible.
